questions.question: What is the fundamental mechanism behind Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
questions.option_a: A. The attacker executes SQL commands directly against the database.
questions.option_b: B. The attacker causes JavaScript to execute in another user's browser within the trusted website's origin.
questions.option_c: C. The attacker modifies the server's operating system configuration.
questions.option_d: D. The attacker intercepts encrypted network traffic.
questions.explanation: XSS occurs when attacker-controlled input is interpreted as executable script by the victim's browser within the trusted site's origin.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes reflected XSS from stored XSS?
questions.option_a: A. Reflected XSS requires database storage, while stored XSS exists only in URL fragments.
questions.option_b: B. Reflected XSS executes only for administrators, while stored XSS executes only for ordinary users.
questions.option_c: C. Reflected XSS is echoed from a request, while stored XSS is persisted by the application and delivered to later visitors.
questions.option_d: D. Reflected XSS executes on the server, while stored XSS executes on the database.
questions.explanation: Reflected XSS returns attacker input directly in the response. Stored XSS saves the payload server-side and executes it whenever users view the affected content.

questions.question: A website displays search results using the following vulnerable PHP code: echo 'Results for ' . $_GET['q'];. What is the primary security issue?
questions.option_a: A. The application executes SQL queries without prepared statements.
questions.option_b: B. User-controlled input is reflected into HTML without context-aware output encoding.
questions.option_c: C. The application exposes its database credentials.
questions.option_d: D. The application accepts unauthorized HTTP methods.
questions.explanation: The search parameter is inserted directly into the response. If it contains HTML or JavaScript, the browser may interpret it as executable content.

questions.question: Which XSS vulnerability is entirely implemented in client-side JavaScript, without requiring the payload to reach the server?
questions.option_a: A. Stored XSS
questions.option_b: B. Reflected XSS
questions.option_c: C. Blind XSS
questions.option_d: D. DOM-based XSS
questions.explanation: DOM-based XSS occurs when client-side JavaScript takes attacker-controlled data from a source and places it into a dangerous sink.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common dangerous sink associated with DOM-based XSS?
questions.option_a: A. innerHTML
questions.option_b: B. textContent
questions.option_c: C. encodeURIComponent
questions.option_d: D. JSON.stringify
questions.explanation: innerHTML interprets supplied content as HTML and may execute event-handler payloads. textContent treats supplied content as text instead.

questions.question: Why can DOM-based XSS remain undetected by server-side request inspection and WAF filtering?
questions.option_a: A. DOM-based XSS always uses encrypted JavaScript.
questions.option_b: B. DOM-based XSS only works when the server disables authentication.
questions.option_c: C. The vulnerable processing can occur entirely in the browser, and URL fragments are not transmitted to the server.
questions.option_d: D. DOM-based XSS does not require attacker-controlled input.
questions.explanation: Client-side sources such as location.hash can be processed locally. URL fragments are not included in HTTP requests, so server-side inspection cannot directly see their contents.

questions.question: What is Blind XSS?
questions.option_a: A. XSS that only works when JavaScript is disabled.
questions.option_b: B. Stored XSS that executes in a location the tester cannot directly observe, such as an administrator dashboard.
questions.option_c: C. XSS that requires the attacker to access the victim's physical device.
questions.option_d: D. XSS that can only modify database records.
questions.explanation: Blind XSS is commonly stored and executes later in an unseen back-office interface. Out-of-band callbacks can confirm execution.

questions.question: Why is Self-XSS generally not considered a valid security finding?
questions.option_a: A. It cannot execute JavaScript.
questions.option_b: B. It only affects websites using HTTP.
questions.option_c: C. It requires the victim to execute the code themselves, without an attacker-controlled delivery path.
questions.option_d: D. It always requires administrator privileges.
questions.explanation: Self-XSS lacks a meaningful attacker-controlled exploitation path. It can become a genuine finding if chained with another vulnerability, such as CSRF.

questions.question: An application reflects user input inside an HTML attribute enclosed in double quotes. Why might a payload designed for the HTML body fail?
questions.option_a: A. JavaScript cannot execute inside HTML attributes.
questions.option_b: B. The browser automatically removes all attacker-controlled characters.
questions.option_c: C. HTML attributes are always protected by CSP.
questions.option_d: D. The payload must first escape the surrounding attribute context before introducing executable content.
questions.explanation: XSS payloads are context-dependent. A payload must break out of the current syntactic context, such as a quoted attribute, before introducing executable HTML or JavaScript.

questions.question: Which security mechanism allows a website to specify which script sources the browser is permitted to execute?
questions.option_a: A. Content Security Policy (CSP)
questions.option_b: B. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
questions.option_c: C. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS)
questions.option_d: D. DNSSEC
questions.explanation: CSP is a response-header-based security mechanism that restricts permitted script sources and can block unauthorized inline scripts.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of setting the HttpOnly attribute on a session cookie?
questions.option_a: A. It prevents all cross-site requests.
questions.option_b: B. It prevents JavaScript from directly accessing the cookie through browser scripting APIs.
questions.option_c: C. It encrypts the cookie value using AES.
questions.option_d: D. It prevents the browser from sending the cookie over HTTPS.
questions.explanation: HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie through interfaces such as document.cookie. It does not prevent XSS from performing authenticated actions.

questions.question: Which approach provides the primary defence against XSS when user-controlled content is included in an HTML page?
questions.option_a: A. Blocking all requests containing the word script.
questions.option_b: B. Validating input only on the client side.
questions.option_c: C. Applying context-aware output encoding at the point where data is inserted.
questions.option_d: D. Disabling database write permissions.
questions.explanation: Context-aware output encoding ensures untrusted data is treated as data rather than executable content in its specific output context.

questions.question: Which statement about CSP is most accurate?
questions.option_a: A. CSP replaces the need for output encoding.
questions.option_b: B. CSP prevents every form of client-side vulnerability.
questions.option_c: C. CSP only protects websites from SQL injection.
questions.option_d: D. CSP is defence in depth, and a weak policy may provide little protection.
questions.explanation: CSP provides an additional browser-side security layer, but it does not replace proper output encoding. Wildcard sources and unsafe directives can weaken its effectiveness.

questions.question: A developer uses React to display user-provided comments. Which implementation choice is more likely to introduce XSS?
questions.option_a: A. Rendering the comment using normal JSX text interpolation.
questions.option_b: B. Rendering the comment using dangerouslySetInnerHTML without appropriate sanitization.
questions.option_c: C. Storing the comment as a database string.
questions.option_d: D. Displaying the comment using a text-only element.
questions.explanation: React normally escapes interpolated text. dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses this protection and can introduce XSS when unsafe HTML is supplied.

questions.question: An attacker injects the payload <scr<script>ipt>alert(1)</script> into an application that removes the first occurrence of the string script only once. Why might this bypass the filter?
questions.option_a: A. The browser ignores all HTML tags containing nested tags.
questions.option_b: B. JavaScript automatically decodes every blocked keyword.
questions.option_c: C. Removing the inner matching text can reconstruct a valid script tag.
questions.option_d: D. CSP automatically converts malformed tags into executable scripts.
questions.explanation: A strip-once blocklist can be bypassed using nested keyword construction. Removing the inner script substring can leave a valid script element.

questions.question: A tester submits an XSS payload that uses because the application blocks script tags. What principle does this demonstrate?
questions.option_a: A. JavaScript can only execute through script elements.
questions.option_b: B. HTML event handlers can execute JavaScript without using a script element.
questions.option_c: C. Image elements execute SQL commands when loading fails.
questions.option_d: D. The browser ignores event handlers on image elements.
questions.explanation: Event-handler attributes such as onerror provide alternative JavaScript execution contexts, so blocking script tags alone is insufficient.

questions.question: A tester discovers that a user-controlled value is placed inside a JavaScript string: var name = 'USER_INPUT';. Which property makes a JavaScript-string-specific XSS payload necessary?
questions.option_a: A. The browser treats the input as a URL.
questions.option_b: B. JavaScript strings cannot contain quotation marks.
questions.option_c: C. The input must escape the surrounding string context before introducing executable JavaScript.
questions.option_d: D. HTML attribute encoding automatically protects JavaScript strings.
questions.explanation: The payload must account for the surrounding JavaScript syntax. Escaping the string context is different from escaping an HTML body or attribute.

questions.question: Which statement best describes Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)?
questions.option_a: A. An attacker injects JavaScript into a database query.
questions.option_b: B. An attacker tricks an authenticated victim's browser into sending an unintended state-changing request.
questions.option_c: C. An attacker directly extracts passwords from the server's memory.
questions.option_d: D. An attacker executes operating system commands through a template engine.
questions.explanation: CSRF abuses the browser's authenticated session to perform an action that the victim did not intend.

questions.question: Why can a malicious website initiate a CSRF attack against a victim who is already logged into another website?
questions.option_a: A. Browsers automatically attach applicable authentication cookies to requests sent to their associated website.
questions.option_b: B. Browsers automatically disclose the victim's password to every visited website.
questions.option_c: C. The Same-Origin Policy disables all authentication checks.
questions.option_d: D. The malicious website can directly read the victim's database session.
questions.explanation: Browsers can automatically attach applicable cookies to requests. CSRF exploits this behaviour to make the target server receive authenticated requests.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes XSS from CSRF?
questions.option_a: A. XSS forges requests, while CSRF injects executable JavaScript into the target page.
questions.option_b: B. XSS executes attacker-controlled script in the victim's browser, while CSRF causes the browser to send an unintended authenticated request.
questions.option_c: C. Both vulnerabilities require database access.
questions.option_d: D. CSRF always provides the attacker with the ability to read the server's response.
questions.explanation: XSS executes attacker-controlled script within the target origin. CSRF abuses authenticated browser requests and generally does not allow the attacker to read the response.

questions.question: Which security control is specifically designed to prevent CSRF by requiring an unpredictable secret associated with the user's session?
questions.option_a: A. Output encoding
questions.option_b: B. Content Security Policy
questions.option_c: C. Anti-CSRF token
questions.option_d: D. SQL parameterization
questions.explanation: A properly validated anti-CSRF token is a secret value that an attacker-controlled external page should not be able to obtain or predict.

questions.question: Why should an application avoid performing state-changing operations through HTTP GET requests?
questions.option_a: A. GET requests cannot contain URL parameters.
questions.option_b: B. GET requests are automatically encrypted.
questions.option_c: C. GET requests cannot be authenticated.
questions.option_d: D. GET requests can be triggered through links and embedded resources, making unintended state changes easier to forge.
questions.explanation: GET should be reserved for retrieving resources. State-changing GET endpoints can be triggered through navigation or elements such as images, creating CSRF opportunities.

questions.question: A web application generates an anti-CSRF token and includes it in every form. However, the server still accepts requests when the token is removed. What is the actual security problem?
questions.option_a: A. The token is too long.
questions.option_b: B. The application does not enforce server-side token validation.
questions.option_c: C. The application uses HTTPS.
questions.option_d: D. The application has enabled SameSite cookies.
questions.explanation: Generating and displaying a token provides no protection if the server does not verify it on state-changing requests.

questions.question: Which combination provides a stronger defence against CSRF?
questions.option_a: A. Client-side validation and JavaScript obfuscation.
questions.option_b: B. CSP and HttpOnly cookies alone.
questions.option_c: C. Validated anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, and avoiding state changes through GET.
questions.option_d: D. Disabling database transactions and enabling verbose logging.
questions.explanation: CSRF protection should combine unpredictable server-validated tokens, appropriate SameSite cookie settings, and safe HTTP method design.

questions.question: A banking application accepts a JSON state-changing endpoint but also accepts requests using text/plain. Why might this be a security concern?
questions.option_a: A. The browser cannot submit text/plain requests.
questions.option_b: B. Some simple cross-origin request mechanisms may reach the endpoint without triggering a CORS preflight.
questions.option_c: C. text/plain automatically encrypts the request body.
questions.option_d: D. JSON endpoints are always vulnerable to SQL injection.
questions.explanation: An endpoint that accepts simple content types such as text/plain may be reachable through cross-origin form-like requests. Correct CSRF protection and content-type validation remain important.

questions.question: A user is authenticated to a banking application. An attacker sends the user a page containing an automatically submitting form that transfers money. The browser sends the session cookie, and the transfer succeeds. Which condition most directly enabled the attack?
questions.option_a: A. The bank allowed the attacker to read its HTML source.
questions.option_b: B. The request was predictable and authenticated using automatically attached cookies without an effective CSRF defence.
questions.option_c: C. The browser disabled JavaScript.
questions.option_d: D. The bank stored the user's password in plaintext.
questions.explanation: The victim's browser supplied the authentication cookie, while the application accepted a predictable state-changing request without an effective unpredictable CSRF token.

questions.question: A security tester finds that a website uses SameSite=Lax cookies. Which statement about this configuration is accurate according to the lecture?
questions.option_a: A. It blocks every cross-site request, including all top-level navigations.
questions.option_b: B. It prevents XSS from executing JavaScript.
questions.option_c: C. It can still allow cookies on top-level cross-site GET navigations, so GET-based state changes remain dangerous.
questions.option_d: D. It makes anti-CSRF tokens unnecessary in every application.
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax generally restricts cross-site cookie sending but allows certain top-level safe-method navigations. A state-changing GET can therefore create a CSRF weakness.

questions.question: What is Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)?
questions.option_a: A. A vulnerability where JavaScript executes in the victim's browser through an HTML event handler.
questions.option_b: B. A vulnerability where attacker-controlled input is embedded into a server-side template and evaluated as a template expression.
questions.option_c: C. A vulnerability where a browser sends an authenticated request without permission.
questions.option_d: D. A vulnerability caused exclusively by weak database passwords.
questions.explanation: SSTI occurs when user input becomes part of the template source rather than being passed as ordinary data.

questions.question: A tester submits {{7*7}} into a display-name field and receives 49 in the response. What does this most strongly indicate?
questions.option_a: A. The application is vulnerable to SQL injection.
questions.option_b: B. The application has successfully encoded the input.
questions.option_c: C. The application may be evaluating user-controlled template expressions.
questions.option_d: D. The application is vulnerable to CSRF.
questions.explanation: The mathematical expression was evaluated instead of displayed literally, indicating possible server-side template injection.

questions.question: Which template syntax is associated with Jinja2 and Twig in the lecture's SSTI fingerprinting table?
questions.explanation: The lecture associates {{7*7}} with Jinja2 and Twig. If evaluated as 49, it indicates that the corresponding template expression syntax may be supported.

questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates SSTI from XSS?
questions.option_a: A. SSTI executes on the server, while XSS executes in the victim's browser.
questions.option_b: B. SSTI always requires an administrator session, while XSS does not.
questions.option_c: C. SSTI is exclusively a database vulnerability, while XSS is a network vulnerability.
questions.option_d: D. Both vulnerabilities only affect browser cookies.
questions.explanation: SSTI occurs during server-side template evaluation and can lead to host-level command execution. XSS executes attacker-controlled JavaScript in the browser.

questions.question: Why can SSTI potentially lead to remote code execution?
questions.option_a: A. Template expressions always contain encrypted passwords.
questions.option_b: B. Template engines can expose the underlying programming language's object model and capabilities, potentially allowing access to operating system functions.
questions.option_c: C. HTML automatically executes operating system commands.
questions.option_d: D. Template engines bypass every operating system permission.
questions.explanation: Certain template engines expose language objects and methods. An attacker may traverse these objects to access functions capable of executing operating system commands.

questions.question: A Python application constructs templates using this pattern: template = 'Hello ' + user_input; render(template). What is the main security problem?
questions.option_a: A. User input is concatenated into the template source, allowing expressions to be evaluated.
questions.option_b: B. The application always produces invalid HTML.
questions.option_c: C. Python automatically converts every input into a database query.
questions.option_d: D. The application cannot process strings.
questions.explanation: Concatenating untrusted input into the template source creates SSTI. The safer design is to use a fixed template and pass user input as a variable.

questions.question: A developer uses a sandboxed template engine to reduce SSTI risk. Which statement best reflects the lecture's security guidance?
questions.option_a: A. Sandboxing makes all template expressions completely harmless.
questions.option_b: B. Sandboxing is a mitigation, but sandbox escapes have historically occurred.
questions.option_c: C. Sandboxing eliminates the need for application updates.
questions.option_d: D. Sandboxing prevents CSRF automatically.
questions.explanation: Sandboxing raises the difficulty of exploitation but is not a guarantee. The structural defence is to keep user input as data and use fixed templates.

questions.question: Which implementation is the most appropriate defence against SSTI?
questions.option_a: A. Remove every occurrence of curly braces from user input.
questions.option_b: B. Allow users to construct templates but disable JavaScript.
questions.option_c: C. Concatenate user input into templates and rely on output encoding.
questions.option_d: D. Use fixed templates, pass user input through template variables, and keep the engine patched.
questions.explanation: Separating template code from user data is the primary defence. Sandboxing and patching provide additional protection.

questions.question: What does insecure deserialization involve?
questions.option_a: A. Converting HTML into CSS without validation.
questions.option_b: B. Reconstructing objects from attacker-controlled serialized data, potentially triggering unintended behaviour.
questions.option_c: C. Sending encrypted network packets without TLS.
questions.option_d: D. Executing SQL statements through prepared queries.
questions.explanation: Deserialization reconstructs objects from serialized data. If that data is attacker-controlled, object creation and method execution can trigger unintended operations.

questions.question: What is a gadget chain in the context of insecure deserialization?
questions.option_a: A. A sequence of existing application classes and methods that can be combined to perform unintended actions.
questions.option_b: B. A sequence of firewall rules used to block malicious requests.
questions.option_c: C. A collection of encrypted session cookies.
questions.option_d: D. A series of HTML elements used to render templates.
questions.explanation: Gadget chains connect existing classes and methods during deserialization to produce harmful behaviour, potentially including remote code execution.

questions.question: Which serialized-data indicator is associated with Java serialization in the lecture?
questions.option_a: A. O:4:"User":..
questions.option_c: C. rO0AB..
questions.option_d: D. ${jndi:ldap://...}
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies the base64 prefix rO0 as a common indicator of Java serialized data.

questions.question: Which Python deserialization mechanism is specifically highlighted as dangerous when used on untrusted data?
questions.option_a: A. json.loads()
questions.option_b: B. pickle.loads()
questions.option_c: C. html.escape()
questions.option_d: D. urllib.parse.quote()
questions.explanation: Python pickle.loads() reconstructs serialized Python objects and can invoke attacker-controlled behaviour through mechanisms such as __reduce__.

questions.question: Which security measure should be performed before deserializing signed serialized data when an integrity mechanism is used?
questions.option_a: A. Execute all object constructors and verify the output afterward.
questions.option_b: B. Decode the object and allow all available classes.
questions.option_c: C. Verify the HMAC or signature before performing deserialization.
questions.option_d: D. Convert the serialized object into HTML.
questions.explanation: Integrity must be verified before deserialization so tampered data is rejected before object reconstruction can trigger malicious behaviour.

questions.question: Which approach is generally preferable when an application needs to exchange ordinary data with clients?
questions.option_a: A. Use native object serialization and allow arbitrary object reconstruction.
questions.option_b: B. Use simple data formats such as JSON with data-only parsing.
questions.option_c: C. Accept arbitrary PHP serialized objects in cookies.
questions.option_d: D. Deserialize all incoming objects before checking their origin.
questions.explanation: Simple formats such as JSON with plain data-only parsers avoid the risks associated with reconstructing arbitrary native objects from untrusted input.

questions.question: A penetration tester discovers that a PHP application accepts a client-controlled serialized object containing an object type and property data. Which function and format are most relevant to investigate?
questions.option_a: A. PHP unserialize() and the O: object notation.
questions.option_b: B. Python pickle.loads() and the rO0AB prefix.
questions.option_c: C. JavaScript innerHTML and the {{7*7}} syntax.
questions.option_d: D. SQL SELECT and the ${jndi:ldap} syntax.
questions.explanation: The lecture associates PHP serialized objects with notation such as O:4:"User":.. and the unserialize() function. Attacker-controlled object reconstruction can lead to object injection and potentially RCE.

questions.question: Which statement best defines a business-logic vulnerability?
questions.option_a: A. An application crashes whenever a user enters an invalid SQL query.
questions.option_b: B. An application correctly executes its code but enforces rules that do not match the intended business requirements.
questions.option_c: C. An application uses an outdated encryption algorithm.
questions.option_d: D. An attacker executes JavaScript inside a browser.
questions.explanation: Business-logic flaws abuse legitimate functionality. Requests may be technically valid, but the application permits actions that violate intended business rules.

questions.question: Why are business-logic vulnerabilities difficult for automated security scanners to identify?
questions.option_a: A. They always require administrator credentials.
questions.option_b: B. They only exist in mobile applications.
questions.option_c: C. They require understanding the intended business process and rules, rather than simply identifying known technical patterns.
questions.option_d: D. They cannot be reproduced using HTTP requests.
questions.explanation: Automated scanners generally lack the business context needed to determine whether an operation violates intended rules, such as quantity limits or payment workflow requirements.

questions.question: An e-commerce application accepts the following request: POST /cart {"item":42,"qty":-3}. The application calculates a negative total and credits the customer's account. What type of vulnerability is demonstrated?
questions.option_a: A. Stored XSS
questions.option_b: B. HTTP request smuggling
questions.option_c: C. Insecure deserialization
questions.option_d: D. Negative quantity business-logic abuse
questions.explanation: The application fails to enforce a valid quantity range. A negative quantity manipulates the business calculation and causes an unintended financial benefit.

questions.question: A checkout endpoint accepts {"item":42,"price":1} and calculates the purchase using the submitted price instead of retrieving the actual product price. What is the primary weakness?
questions.option_a: A. The server trusts a client-controlled business value.
questions.option_b: B. The server uses an insecure template engine.
questions.option_c: C. The browser has disabled SameSite cookies.
questions.option_d: D. The application has a missing Content Security Policy.
questions.explanation: The client must not determine authoritative product prices. The server should retrieve the actual price and calculate the total independently.

questions.question: A shopping application permits customers to submit the same single-use discount voucher multiple times. Which security control most directly addresses this issue?
questions.option_a: A. HTML output encoding.
questions.option_b: B. Server-side enforcement of one-use voucher rules.
questions.option_c: C. Enabling directory listing.
questions.option_d: D. Disabling HTTP POST requests.
questions.explanation: Voucher usage limits must be enforced by the server. The application should track redemption state and prevent repeated use.

questions.question: A multi-step checkout process is intended to follow cart → payment → confirmation. A tester directly submits a request to the confirmation endpoint without completing payment, and the order is confirmed. What is the underlying vulnerability?
questions.option_a: A. Missing HTTP response compression.
questions.option_b: B. Reflected XSS.
questions.option_c: C. Workflow or process-step bypass.
questions.option_d: D. Weak password hashing.
questions.explanation: The application trusts the client to follow the intended workflow. A server-side state machine should verify that the required previous steps have been completed.

questions.question: What does TOCTOU stand for in the context of race conditions?
questions.option_a: A. Time of Cookie to Time of User
questions.option_b: B. Transfer of Control to Transfer of Ownership
questions.option_c: C. Type of Check to Type of Output
questions.option_d: D. Time of Check to Time of Use
questions.explanation: TOCTOU describes a vulnerability where a condition is checked and an action is performed later, leaving a window in which the underlying state can change.

questions.question: An application checks whether a voucher has been redeemed and then marks it as used in a separate operation. Multiple parallel requests arrive before the voucher status is updated. What can happen?
questions.option_a: A. All requests are automatically rejected because HTTP is stateless.
questions.option_b: B. Several requests may pass the initial check and redeem the supposedly single-use voucher multiple times.
questions.option_c: C. The browser automatically encrypts the voucher.
questions.option_d: D. The database automatically detects all business-logic violations.
questions.explanation: The check and update are not atomic. Multiple concurrent requests may observe the same unused state and successfully redeem the voucher.

questions.question: Which approach most directly prevents race conditions involving shared balances or single-use vouchers?
questions.option_a: A. Perform the check and state-changing operation atomically using database transactions or appropriate locking.
questions.option_b: B. Increase the number of frontend validation rules.
questions.option_c: C. Add a Content Security Policy header.
questions.option_d: D. Hide the redemption button after the first click.
questions.explanation: Atomic transactions or locks ensure that checking and updating shared state occur as one protected operation, preventing competing requests from exploiting the gap.

questions.question: A penetration tester wants to identify business-logic flaws in an online payment system. Which testing strategy is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: A. Only scan for known CVEs in JavaScript libraries.
questions.option_b: B. Only enumerate open TCP ports.
questions.option_c: C. Map the intended payment workflow and test impossible values, out-of-order actions, repeated operations, and parallel requests.
questions.option_d: D. Only search the HTML source for script tags.
questions.explanation: Business-logic testing requires understanding the intended process and challenging its assumptions through invalid values, workflow manipulation, and concurrency testing.

questions.question: A web application uses a server-side state machine for checkout. What should happen when a client submits a confirmation request before completing payment?
questions.option_a: A. The server should accept the request because the client is authenticated.
questions.option_b: B. The server should verify the required previous state and reject the invalid transition.
questions.option_c: C. The server should execute the confirmation request twice.
questions.option_d: D. The server should redirect the request to the homepage without checking payment status.
questions.explanation: A server-side state machine enforces valid workflow transitions independently of the client's navigation sequence.

questions.question: What is security misconfiguration?
questions.option_a: A. A vulnerability caused exclusively by incorrect database normalization.
questions.option_b: B. A situation where an application or its supporting infrastructure is deployed with insecure settings.
questions.option_c: C. A vulnerability where client input is interpreted as a template expression.
questions.option_d: D. A problem caused only by weak session identifiers.
questions.explanation: Security misconfiguration includes insecure defaults, exposed debugging features, excessive permissions, missing security headers, and improperly configured infrastructure.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of security misconfiguration?
questions.option_a: A. An application using parameterized SQL queries.
questions.option_b: B. An application implementing server-side output encoding.
questions.option_c: C. A production server exposing verbose stack traces and debug mode.
questions.option_d: D. An application enforcing transaction atomicity.
questions.explanation: Exposing debug mode and verbose error information in production can disclose internal implementation details and assist attackers.

questions.question: Which combination contains only examples of security misconfiguration discussed in the lecture?
questions.option_a: A. Default credentials, directory listing, exposed admin consoles, and world-readable cloud storage.
questions.option_b: B. SQL parameterization, output encoding, HMAC verification, and atomic transactions.
questions.option_c: C. Stored XSS, DOM XSS, SSTI, and reflected XSS.
questions.option_d: D. Race conditions, coupon stacking, negative quantities, and workflow bypass.
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies default credentials, directory listing, exposed administrative interfaces, and insecure cloud storage permissions as common misconfigurations.

questions.question: An application developer discovers that the application code is secure but a third-party dependency contains a publicly documented vulnerability. Which OWASP category is most directly associated with this issue in the lecture?
questions.option_a: A. A05: Security Misconfiguration
questions.option_b: B. A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
questions.option_c: C. A03: Injection
questions.option_d: D. A01: Broken Access Control
questions.explanation: A06 concerns vulnerable and outdated components. Third-party dependencies can introduce known vulnerabilities even when the application's own code is secure.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an SBOM in dependency security?
questions.option_a: A. To list all users who have authenticated to the application.
questions.option_b: B. To store session cookies and encryption keys.
questions.option_c: C. To provide an inventory of software components and dependencies used by an application.
questions.option_d: D. To automatically remove all vulnerable application code.
questions.explanation: A Software Bill of Materials provides visibility into the components and dependencies included in software, helping identify exposure to known vulnerabilities.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) as presented in the lecture?
questions.option_a: A. It was an XSS vulnerability caused by unsafe HTML rendering.
questions.option_b: B. It affected a logging library that could resolve attacker-controlled JNDI lookups, potentially resulting in unauthenticated remote code execution.
questions.option_c: C. It was a CSRF vulnerability caused by missing SameSite cookies.
questions.option_d: D. It was a race condition in Java database transactions.
questions.explanation: Log4Shell affected Log4j and allowed attacker-controlled JNDI lookups to trigger remote class retrieval and execution under vulnerable conditions.

questions.question: Why can a malicious Log4Shell payload be supplied through a User-Agent header?
questions.option_a: A. The User-Agent header is always interpreted as JavaScript by browsers.
questions.option_b: B. HTTP headers are automatically converted into SQL statements.
questions.option_c: C. Application components may log attacker-controlled header values, triggering vulnerable Log4j lookup processing.
questions.option_d: D. The User-Agent header bypasses all network authentication mechanisms.
questions.explanation: If a vulnerable application logs attacker-controlled values such as User-Agent, Log4j may process the malicious JNDI lookup during logging.

questions.question: Which tools are specifically mentioned in the lecture for identifying vulnerable or outdated dependencies?
questions.option_a: A. Nmap and Hydra
questions.option_b: B. XSStrike and Turbo Intruder
questions.option_c: C. Wireshark and tcpdump
questions.option_d: D. retire.js and OWASP Dependency-Check
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies retire.js and OWASP Dependency-Check as tools for detecting vulnerable dependencies and outdated components.

questions.question: What is the fundamental cause of HTTP request smuggling?
questions.option_a: A. A browser automatically sends session cookies to every website.
questions.option_b: B. A front-end proxy and back-end server disagree about where an HTTP request ends.
questions.option_c: C. An application accepts negative product quantities.
questions.option_d: D. A server executes untrusted template expressions.
questions.explanation: Request smuggling occurs when HTTP request boundaries are interpreted differently by front-end and back-end components, allowing hidden requests to pass through.

questions.question: Which HTTP headers are central to the classic CL.TE and TE.CL request-smuggling techniques?
questions.option_a: A. Host and Cookie
questions.option_b: B. Referer and User-Agent
questions.option_c: C. Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
questions.option_d: D. Authorization and Accept
questions.explanation: CL.TE and TE.CL arise from disagreements over Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding when determining HTTP request boundaries.

questions.question: In a CL.TE request-smuggling scenario, which parsing behaviour does the name describe?
questions.option_a: A. The front-end uses Content-Length while the back-end uses Transfer-Encoding.
questions.option_b: B. The front-end uses Transfer-Encoding while the back-end uses Content-Length.
questions.option_c: C. Both servers exclusively use Content-Length.
questions.option_d: D. Both servers exclusively use Transfer-Encoding.
questions.explanation: CL.TE means the front-end uses Content-Length and the back-end uses Transfer-Encoding, potentially causing the two systems to disagree about request boundaries.

questions.question: What is a possible consequence of successful HTTP request smuggling?
questions.option_a: A. Automatic correction of all HTTP request headers.
questions.option_b: B. Prevention of all cache-related vulnerabilities.
questions.option_c: C. Automatic encryption of requests between users.
questions.option_d: D. Front-end security bypass, cache poisoning, or interference with another user's request.
questions.explanation: Request smuggling can bypass front-end controls and cause the back-end to process unintended requests, potentially affecting subsequent users.

questions.question: An HTTP request contains both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding. What is a suitable mitigation against ambiguity in request parsing?
questions.option_a: A. Allow every intermediary to interpret the request independently.
questions.option_b: B. Reject ambiguous requests and ensure consistent parsing across the entire proxy and server chain.
questions.option_c: C. Disable authentication on the back-end server.
questions.option_d: D. Increase the Content-Length value until both servers accept the request.
questions.explanation: The request-processing chain should agree on message boundaries. Rejecting ambiguous Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding combinations reduces desynchronisation risks.

questions.question: Which activity belongs primarily to the Design phase of the secure SDLC described in the lecture?
questions.option_a: A. Threat modelling, secure requirements, and abuse cases.
questions.option_b: B. Dependency scanning and secret scanning.
questions.option_c: C. Penetration testing and DAST.
questions.option_d: D. Logging, alerting, and incident response.
questions.explanation: The Design phase establishes security requirements, performs threat modelling, and identifies abuse cases before implementation.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly represents the secure SDLC phases presented in the lecture?
questions.option_a: A. Build → Design → Deploy → Code → Monitor → Test
questions.option_b: B. Design → Code → Build → Test → Deploy → Monitor
questions.option_c: C. Code → Build → Design → Monitor → Deploy → Test
questions.option_d: D. Test → Deploy → Design → Code → Build → Monitor
questions.explanation: The lecture presents the sequence Design, Code, Build, Test, Deploy, and Monitor, with security controls integrated throughout.

questions.question: Which security activity is most closely associated with the Build phase of the secure SDLC?
questions.option_a: A. Threat modelling and secure requirements.
questions.option_b: B. Penetration testing and dynamic application testing.
questions.option_c: C. Dependency scanning and secret scanning.
questions.option_d: D. Incident response and security alerting.
questions.explanation: The Build phase includes Software Composition Analysis (SCA) and secret scanning to identify vulnerable dependencies and exposed credentials.

questions.question: A company discovers XSS vulnerabilities during a production penetration test. It wants to prevent similar vulnerabilities from being introduced in future development. Which SDLC activities are most directly relevant?
questions.option_a: A. Code-stage secure coding, output encoding, SAST, and code review.
questions.option_b: B. Monitor-stage logging and incident response only.
questions.option_c: C. Deploy-stage firewall configuration only.
questions.option_d: D. Build-stage dependency scanning only.
questions.explanation: The Code phase includes secure coding, output encoding, static analysis, and code review, helping prevent XSS before deployment.

questions.question: Which statement best captures the central security principle connecting the three parts of the Web Application Security lecture?
questions.option_a: A. Every web vulnerability can be eliminated by installing a WAF.
questions.option_b: B. All vulnerabilities originate from weak password hashing.
questions.option_c: C. Web security depends primarily on hiding application source code.
questions.option_d: D. Applications repeatedly become vulnerable when they trust client-controlled identity, input, browser behaviour, or business values.
questions.explanation: The lecture's synthesis identifies misplaced trust in client-controlled information as a common root cause across access-control, injection, browser-side, and business-logic vulnerabilities.
